newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court broadens workplace anti-bias law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court broadens workplace anti-bias law.

text.p: A unanimous Supreme Court ruled Tuesday that former employees are covered under the anti-retaliation provisions of a federal civil rights law protecting workers who file discrimination claims.
In an opinion by Justice Clarence Thomas the court said protections against retaliation under the 1964 federal civil rights law involving workers extended to former employees.

The case was brought by Charles Robinson, a mid-Atlantic sales representative who was fired in 1991 by Shell Oil Co., his employer of more than 11 years. Robinson, who is black, alleged in a complaint filed with the federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission that he was fired because of his race.

He applied for a job with Metropolitan Life Insurance Co., which contacted Shell for a reference. Shell, a unit of Royal Dutch/Shell Group ( ), replied that Robinson had been fired, said it would not re-employ him and rated him as below-average in nine employment categories, with his attendance rated poor.
Robinson, alleging that Shell provided the poor reference and false information in retaliation for his discrimination claim, then filed a second complaint for alleged retaliation.

Shell argued that the law protects only "employees or applicants for employment" from retaliation for the filing of bias claims. A federal judge and a U.S. appeals court agreed that the law did not cover former employees.

Thomas acknowledged the meaning of employees in one section was "ambiguous," but in the "broader context" of the law and its primary purpose, he concluded the law does include former employees and Robinson's lawsuit may proceed.

Thomas said several sections of the law plainly contemplate that former employees be covered, including the section barring a discriminatory firing. He said the EEOC argued that excluding former employees would undermine the law's effectiveness and provide a "perverse incentive" for employers to fire workers who might bring a bias claim.
The decision resolved conflicting lower-court rulings on the issue. The Justice Department and a number of civil rights groups had urged the high court to rule that the law covers former employees.
In other unanimous rulings, the Supreme Court:

-- decided that a California regulation involving wages paid to employees in apprenticeship programs was not preempted by federal law. The state law requires payment of prevailing wages in programs that have not received state approval but allows payment of lower appreticeship wages to employees participating in state-approved programs that meet federal standards.

-- ruled for the Internal Revenue Service and said people who overpay their federal income taxes cannot get a refund after missing the filing deadline, even if they claim a mental disability had caused the delay.
